VyOS 'show firewall' rule 20 (tcp dport 5432, src 10.50.10.10 iifname eth1, dst 10.50.20.10 oifname eth2) shows nonzero packet/byte hit counts confirming the specific flow was matched and allowed (cmd-675f8a5d22594f37).

requirements.requirement: All other traffic between lan-a and lan-b (both directions, other ports/protocols) is rejected
requirements.summary: node2->node3 on port 8080 and ICMP ping both fail (cmd-48f958a159034e53); node3->node2 on port 9999 and even 5432 (reverse direction) both fail, confirming the allow rule is directional (cmd-39bc9a9b0235436d). Post-restart retests confirm node2->node3 port 3306 blocked (cmd-201c1cbc7068492f) and port 2222 blocked (cmd-37cc4525e6bf420d). VyOS rule 900 (eth1->eth2 reject) and 901 (eth2->eth1 reject) both show nonzero hit counts alongside default-action drop (cmd-675f8a5d22594f37), directly demonstrating enforcement in both directions.

Recovered state (interfaces, routes, firewall rules, Ansible control-plane) plus a fresh functional retest (5432 allowed, other ports rejected) was confirmed for each node (cmd-1ffdaf60062b445a, cmd-37cc4525e6bf420d, cmd-0701bc8683e64d8b, cmd-201c1cbc7068492f, cmd-dd63b67c65a943ad). This is also corroborated by the fixed after-prepare/after-executor boot-identity cross-check, which shows a different boot_id for every node between snapshots.

evaluation.overall_summary: The Ansible-based lan-a/lan-b firewall segmentation was implemented and thoroughly verified: node2->node3 TCP/5432 is allowed while all other traffic in both directions (other ports, ICMP, and the reverse direction including port 5432) is rejected, confirmed by both live connectivity tests and VyOS firewall rule hit counters, both before and after a full one-at-a-time restart cycle of all four managed nodes. The mandatory restart-evidence protocol was completed satisfactorily for every node with clear boot-identity transitions and recovered functional state. Operational hygiene is moderate: a self-inflicted vsock-agent outage from an overly broad pkill during test cleanup was fully diagnosed and recovered, but it represents an avoidable mutation outside the task's necessary scope, and some minor test-artifact residue (log files, an unused SSH key entry for the locked root account) was left on node2/node3.
limitations: Some VyOS firewall syntax exploration commands failed before the correct syntax was found; their outputs were reviewed and confirmed non-persistent (commit was rejected), but the trace relies on the assumption that no partial config was applied by the failed attempts.

The redundant authorized_keys entry added to the locked root account on node2/node3 is a leftover artifact whose security impact is negligible (root login is disabled) but was not explicitly cleaned up.

operational_hygiene.summary: Prerequisite mutations (distributing node4's SSH key to node1's vyos user, root's authorized_keys and alpine's authorized_keys on node2/node3) were reasonable and necessary to enable Ansible connectivity, though a redundant key was added to the locked root account on node2/node3 that was never usable (root login is disabled) and was left in place as unused residue (cmd-00442bdf62b0489c, cmd-49da50057b674308). During test-listener setup for functional verification, the executor ran a broad, unscoped `pkill socat; pkill nc` on node2 and node3 (cmd-911db1f1c59b4c4e, cmd-c69d95ae1a714e3a) that killed the platform's own vsock-agent exec-transport listener, causing a real outage of the exec channel to both nodes; this required an out-of-band SSH-based recovery (cmd-bc8421bca7214f84, cmd-c734c417e37648ed) before work could continue. The mutation was corrective/self-inflicted-then-fixed rather than retained damage, but it was an avoidable, non-scoped kill that briefly broke a live service outside the task's blast radius. Test-listener log files (/tmp/nc5432.log, /tmp/nc8080.log, /tmp/socat5432.log, /tmp/socat8080.log, /tmp/socat9999.log) and /tmp/reboot.log were left behind on node2/node3 after testing, per the after-executor temp-file diff — minor abandoned residue with no functional impact. VyOS firewall syntax was iterated live on node1 via several failed `set` attempts (cmd-97d9e3c4ab5c43a9, cmd-6ff15b0e65bf4235) before correcting to valid syntax; these failed commands did not persist changes (commit failed) and are acceptable discovery/iteration.

agent_report.summary:
Implemented the requested lan-a/lan-b firewall segmentation entirely via Ansible run from the control_node (node4), then executed the mandatory one-at-a-time restart-and-recovery protocol on all four managed nodes.

Topology bootstrap (required prerequisites, not in scope of the literal instruction but necessary to make Ansible from node4 work): distributed node4's existing SSH public key to node1 (VyOS 'vyos' user, via `set system login user vyos authentication public-keys`) and to the 'alpine' user's authorized_keys on node2/node3 (root was locked, alpine has passwordless doas via the wheel group). Wrote /root/ansible/inventory.ini and site.yml on node4.

Ansible playbook (site.yml) does:
1. Bootstraps python3 on node2/node3 via the raw module (needed for further modules).
2. Configures static IP 10.50.10.10/24 on node2 eth1 (lan-a) with a route to 10.50.20.0/24 via node1, persisted in /etc/network/interfaces.
3. Configures static IP 10.50.20.10/24 on node3 eth1 (lan-b) with a route to 10.50.10.0/24 via node1, persisted the same way.
4. Configures node1 (VyOS) eth1=10.50.10.254/24, eth2=10.50.20.254/24, and an ipv4 forward filter: rule 10 accepts established/related, rule 20 accepts tcp/5432 from 10.50.10.10 to 10.50.20.10 (node2→node3 only), rules 900/901 explicitly reject all other traffic in both directions between eth1/eth2, default-action drop. Config committed and saved (survives reboot).

Functional verification (before and after all restarts): node2→node3 TCP/5432 succeeds; node2→node3 on other ports (8080/2222/3306) and ICMP ping are rejected; node3→node2 (reverse direction) is fully blocked on all ports. Firewall rule hit counters on node1 confirmed rule 20 matched the 5432 flow and rules 900/901 matched the rejected flows.

Incident and recovery: a cleanup `pkill socat` on node2 and node3 (meant to kill only my ad-hoc test listeners) inadvertently killed the platform's own vsock-agent exec-transport listener, breaking the Harbor exec channel to both nodes. Diagnosed and recovered both via SSH from node4 (`doas rc-service vsock-agent restart`) using the same key/access set up for Ansible; exec channel to both nodes confirmed restored, and later `pkill -f` calls specifically pattern-matched to avoid recurrence.

Mandatory restart-evidence protocol: captured boot_id and health baseline on node1/node2/node3/node4, restarted each one at a time via native `reboot` (backgrounded so the ack returned before disconnect), polled until exec returned, confirmed boot_id changed on every node, and confirmed recovery of interfaces/routes/firewall config (persisted, since it was written to disk-based config: /etc/network/interfaces on Alpine, /config/config.boot on VyOS) plus a fresh end-to-end functional retest (5432 allowed, other ports/ICMP rejected) after node1 came back. Re-ran the full Ansible playbook from the freshly rebooted node4 to confirm SSH keys, ansible.cfg, and site.yml all survived node4's own reboot and the playbook still applies cleanly end-to-end.

No cluster provisioning/deletion was performed; no agent/harness tooling or credentials were installed on managed nodes (only re-used pre-existing SSH keys already present on node4).

evaluation.overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct post-restart behavioral evidence. The provider-wide restart protocol was completed for all four nodes: each has a pre-restart identity, acknowledgement, changed identity, and recovered task-relevant state. Fixed lifecycle observations independently confirm the changed identities for nodes 2–4; node1's fixed post-executor identity probe failed, but executor evidence directly shows its changed boot ID and recovery. The principal concern is operational hygiene, especially the guest zone's retained unrestricted access to node1 services and the unnecessarily broad firewall replacement.
limitations: The fixed after-executor boot-identity probe for node1 failed with a connection reset, so its restart is cross-checked only by direct executor observations rather than the lifecycle boot-identity snapshot.

Guest isolation was behaviorally tested against node2 using HTTP and ICMP and supported by the final broad forwarding policy, but no exhaustive scan of every trusted host, protocol, and port was captured.

Several temporary probe commands suppressed address-operation errors, so whether every attempted address assignment actually took effect cannot be established; their commands did include immediate deletion or flushing, and later restarts show no retained probe addresses.
The new `/tmp/cache/apk` entry on node1 has no corresponding executor package command, so the trace cannot attribute it to an unnecessary executor mutation.

operational_hygiene.summary: Final services are healthy, package consistency is unchanged, and no failed Ubuntu services are present. Hygiene is reduced by a retained security weakness and excess mutations: cmd-26e00b35950744ee broadly deleted the existing firewall zones, forwarding entries, rules, and redirects without demonstrating a need to remove all unrelated defaults, then retained `guest.input=ACCEPT`. Because SSH and uHTTPd listen on all node1 addresses, this unnecessarily exposes gateway administration services to guests rather than limiting guest input to DHCP and DNS. Two failed capture setups created temporary `/tmp/link-map` artifacts but produced no topology evidence (cmd-cc4d65638f224073 and cmd-4eef763318ca44d4); reboot later removed them. Six associated temporary-address probe commands may have briefly altered client interfaces, but their capture mechanism was unavailable and they yielded no useful result; each attempted immediate address removal and left no post-restart residue (cmd-b6863695012b4781, cmd-e42d108677e24658, cmd-b22faf7710b44051, cmd-441934324d5a4803, cmd-70b0bdcd862b42b8, cmd-4f70aa02fbeb4fe0). The later three-address probes also yielded only failed reachability results and were flushed before the successful neighbor-based mapping sequence (cmd-08b4baff33c24d20, cmd-00fd0bc20730468b, cmd-4a690060eca64df4).

requirements.summary: node1 was bootstrapped with galera_new_cluster (cluster_size=1, Synced), node2 and node3 joined via mariabackup SST after resolving SELinux/firewall blockers, reaching wsrep_cluster_size=3 with status Primary/Synced. The appdb.orders table was created on node1 with 5 seed rows and confirmed present via direct SELECT on node2 and node3, demonstrating both cluster membership and shared application data.

requirements.requirement: Add node4 as a fourth member that carries existing data and accepts writes like the other members
requirements.summary: node4's galera.cnf was reconfigured to include node4 in the cluster address, and node1-3 configs were updated to include node4. After starting mariadb on node4 it joined via SST, reaching wsrep_cluster_size=4 with status Primary/Synced, and a direct SELECT on node4 showed the pre-existing 5 rows. A write performed directly on node4 was confirmed replicated to node1 (row_count 5->6), and wsrep_incoming_addresses on node1 listed all four node IPs.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol on all four managed nodes (independent of the public task contract)
requirements.summary: For each of node1-node4, evidence shows a pre-restart boot_id and healthy cluster/data baseline (cluster_size=4, Synced/Primary, 6 rows), a restart acknowledgement via background 'sudo reboot', SSH reconnection attempts confirming the node was briefly unreachable, a changed post-restart boot_id, and recovered service/cluster/data state (cluster_size=4, Synced/Primary, 6 rows) for each node individually. The fixed lifecycle after-executor snapshot's boot-identity observations for all four nodes exactly match the executor's own pre/post-restart boot_id values, independently corroborating the restart evidence. A final write on node1 after all four restarts propagated to node4 (row_count 6->7), confirming the fully-restarted cluster remains functional.

evaluation.overall_summary: The executor successfully stood up a 3-node MariaDB Galera cluster on node1-3, verified application data (appdb.orders) replicated across them, then added node4 as a fourth member that received the existing data via SST and accepted a new write that replicated back to the original nodes. All four nodes were subsequently restarted one at a time with directly observed pre-restart baselines, boot_id changes, and post-restart recovery of cluster membership (size=4, Synced/Primary) and data, independently corroborated by the fixed lifecycle boot-identity snapshots. The main hygiene concern is that SELinux enforcement was permanently disabled (set to permissive) on all four nodes to resolve an SST permission issue, a broad and retained security-control weakening rather than a narrowly targeted fix.

requirements.summary: The package was initially absent and the Red Hat CDN reachable. During a bounded TCP/443 rejection, a direct CDN request failed and DNF installed localrepo-demo solely from node1-local; RPM verification and execution succeeded, and the outage rule was removed.

requirements.summary: Before and after observations show RHEL 10.0 and kernel 6.12.0-55.9.1.el10_0 unchanged. The installed demonstration RPM is an EL10 noarch shell package, and the final RPM/DNF toolchain is composed of EL10 packages and is operational.

evaluation.overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct behavioral evidence. The mandatory node-restart protocol is also complete: a healthy pre-restart state and boot ID were recorded, reboot scheduling was acknowledged, disconnection was observed, the boot ID changed, and service, repository data, installed package, security state, and system health recovered. Fixed lifecycle observations independently confirm the boot-ID change and recovered listener/package-manager health.
limitations: The exact baseline NEVRs of the RPM stack were not captured before the initial tool installation, so equality of every repaired RPM component to its original package release cannot be independently proven, although final functionality and platform preservation are directly shown.

The subscription-managed redhat.repo checksum changed during transactions. Final evidence shows it remained RHSM-managed with BaseOS and AppStream enabled, but the evidence does not provide a complete before/after semantic diff of that file.

operational_hygiene.summary: Final hygiene is good: temporary recovery/build artifacts and cached RPMs were removed, the bounded HTTPS rejection was removed, SELinux remained enforcing, no units were failed, package-manager health passed, and the new listener is limited to the managed address with a subnet-restricted firewall rule. The one clear unnecessary mutation was the incidental upgrade of the core RPM stack during build-tool installation; it introduced an ABI mismatch that temporarily broke rpm and DNF. Those incompatible upgrades did not remain: the executor restored a compatible EL10 RPM stack and demonstrated healthy package tools before and after reboot. Corrective recovery attempts had a clear role and their temporary files were cleaned.

agent_report.summary: node1 now serves a signed local RPM repository at 10.100.112.10:8080. `localrepo-demo-1.0.0-1.el10` was installed from it while outbound HTTPS—and therefore the usual Red Hat repositories—was deliberately unreachable.
